title: Alone or Together?
blurb: Talk about housing and living arrangements

steps.html:
Twenty households in Leeds share one laundry and a garden. Forty-seven per cent of Swedish homes contain exactly one person. Two texts about how we live, and the small words that decide whether you mean few or a few.

  • Read two texts about housing and compare their arguments
  • Use few / a few, most of, neither of, plenty of accurately
  • Describe numbers and proportions in words
  • Write about how people live where you are

steps.title: Before you read: what would put you off co-housing?

options.label: Not being able to sell and move

steps.title: Twenty front doors and one laundry
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 147 words

Lilac is a co-housing project in Leeds. Every household has its own private flat or house, with its own front door, its own kitchen and its own bathroom. What the residents share is the rest: a laundry, a garden, an entertainment space and a large kitchen for evenings when several families eat together.

Most of the residents came for the same reason, and it was not money. A few of them have said publicly that they had been living independently for years and had found it quieter than they wanted.

Few of them describe the project as a commune, and none of them has to eat with anybody. Twice a week a meal is cooked for whoever turns up; plenty of people never come.

The property is owned jointly, which means that neither of the two families who left last year could simply sell up and go.

options: A laundry, a kitchen, a bathroom and a front door for each household.
A laundry, a garden, an entertainment space and a large shared kitchen.

steps.title: The world's fastest-growing household
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 145 words

Globally, the number of people living alone has risen faster over the last thirty years than any other kind of household. In Sweden, forty-seven per cent of homes now have just one resident. Most people do not guess that correctly.

The fastest growth, however, is not in Europe. It is in China, India and Brazil, where a great many young adults now move out of the family home before marriage — something very few of their grandparents did.

Several explanations are offered. A little more money, a lot more privacy, a great deal more choice. Each of them explains some of the rise; none of them explains all of it.

What almost nobody in the data is doing is choosing to be alone. Living independently and living separately are not the same thing, and most of the people in these figures see somebody every day.

steps.title: How much, how many, and how you feel about it
steps.html:
The full picture, then the two distinctions that decide B2 accuracy.

Some quantifiers go only with countable nouns (many, few, a few, several, a number of), some only with uncountable (much, little, a little, a great deal of), and some with either (a lot of, plenty of, most, some, no, all).

The first distinction: few against a few. A few means 'some, and that is a reasonable number'. Few means 'almost none', and it carries a negative judgement. The same applies to little and a little: a little time is enough, little time is not.

The second: of or no of. Use of only when you are talking about a specific, already-identified group: most of the residents, few of them. With a general statement, drop it: most residents, few people.

Each, every, neither, either, none are singular and take a singular verb: Each of them explains some of it. None of them explains all of it. Neither of the two families was able to sell.

For describing data, the usual phrases are the majority of, a significant proportion of, roughly a third of, just under half of, almost nobody.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences from the two texts.

Most of the residents came for the same reason.
A specific group → of.

Most people guess the figure wrongly.
A general statement → no of.

A few of them have said so publicly.
Some, and worth mentioning.

Few of them describe it as a commune.
Almost none. Negative in tone.

None of them has to eat with anybody.
Singular verb after none of.

Plenty of people never come.
More than enough — with a countable plural.

Neither of the two families was able to sell.
Two only, and singular.

Each of them explains some of the rise.
Singular verb after each of.

A great many young adults move out before marriage.
Countable, emphatic.

A little more money, a lot more privacy.
A little + comparative; uncountable.

Very few of their grandparents did.
Very few intensifies the 'almost none'.

Almost nobody in the data is choosing to be alone.
Useful for describing figures.

steps.title: Choosing between few and a few, with and without of
steps.html:
1. You want to say that a small number of residents call it a commune, and that you think it is a very small number.
  2. Small number, negative judgement → few, not a few.
  3. Are you talking about a specific group already named? Yes — the residents of Lilac. So you need of: few of them.
  4. Result: Few of them describe it as a commune.
  5. Now change the meaning: some residents did say it, and you find that worth reporting → A few of them described it as a commune. One letter, and the sentence has changed sides.

steps.title: Write your description.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use at least five different quantifiers, and at least one contrast between few and a few, or little and a little.
steps.placeholder: Most of the flats in my …
steps.html:
• Open with a general statement using <i>most</i>.
  • Use <i>a few</i> and <i>few</i> in the same paragraph, to mean different things.
  • Give one number, described in words: <i>roughly a third of…</i>
  • Use <i>neither</i> or <i>none</i> with a singular verb.
  • Close with a comparison across generations.

Useful language

  • Most of the flats in my building are …
  • A few of my neighbours … , but few of them …
  • Plenty of people here …
  • Neither of my grandparents ever …
  • Roughly a third of … / Just under half of …
  • Almost nobody I know …
steps.modelHtml:
Nine floors, one lift

Most of the flats in my building were bought in the 1990s, and a great many of them are still lived in by the same families. That is unusual now. Few of my friends have stayed anywhere for more than four years.

A few of my neighbours know each other well — the four women on the second floor have been organising the courtyard for decades. Plenty of people, though, have never spoken to anybody above the fifth floor. Neither of the families next to me was here when I moved in.

Roughly a third of the flats now have one resident, which would have been unthinkable to my grandmother. Almost nobody I know under thirty lives with their parents once they are working, and very few of them plan to.
